newsitem.title: UK: Calling "Independence Day" aliens--TODAY'S the Day.
newsitem.headline: Calling "Independence Day" aliens--TODAY'S the Day.

text.p: November 5, 1996, looked a good day for aliens to attack planet Earth, with the world's sole superpower and its largest country preoccupied deciding their future in election booths and on the operating table.
As the United States voted for president and Russia's leader Boris Yeltsin underwent heart surgery, both countries turned inwards and the world's political pulse slowed perceptibly.

War in Afghanistan, humanitarian disaster in central Africa and tension in the Middle East persisted but, for 24 hours, two countries whose Cold War formed the backbone of world history for 40 years concentrated solely on internal affairs.
It's virtually an alternative prologue for the blockbuster Hollywood film, "Independence Day" about invading creatures who launch a coordinated attack from enormous space ships.
They destroy cities, but the aliens are ultimately defeated after the world's nations join together with patriotic Americans.
U.S. President Bill Clinton was strong favourite to beat Republican challenger Bob Dole and win the right to lead 260 million Americans into the new millennium.
"This is the greatest country in human history because we have created a system in which you are the boss," Clinton told voters in his last campaign speech.

While American voters held their country's future in their hands, surgeons in Moscow were deciding with their scalpels whether Yeltsin's heart would recover sufficiently for him to resume full power in Russia.
Surgeons say he had more than the forecast three or four heart bypasses, but the seven-hour operation was a success and he would be able to resume normal work.
Meanwhile, the reins of power were held by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Political analysts speculated Yeltsin's operation had been deliberately timed to coincide with polling day in the United States in a bid to deflect media scrutiny away from the Kremlin.

The 65-year-old's effectiveness has been badly hobbled by a weak heart for several months. Tuesday's surgery will determine whether he regains the vigour he showed when defying coup plotters astride a tank in 1991, or be forced to stand down.

Health is also a major preoccupation in China where Deng Xiaoping, paramount leader of 1.2 billion people in the world's most populous nation, has not been seen in public since early February 1994. Television film then showed him at a Lunar New Year reception in Shanghai.

The death of Deng, 92, would almost certainly lead to a scramble for power in China and, like a change of president in the United States or the departure of Yeltsin, trigger seismic changes in international relations.
Elsewhere in the world's major capitals, domestic politics concentrated the minds of the political elite.
In Japan, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tried to put together a cabinet after being forced to form a minority government following his failure to agree a new coalition.

The dismissal of Pakistan Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto caused a few flutters in Britain, the former colonial power in the region, but Prime Minister John Major's government was more intent on preserving power than overseas politics.
Facing an election by May, Major's cabinet met to discuss public spending plans ahead of the 1997 budget, a subject that also occupied the thoughts of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Kohl was holed up on Tuesday morning with his cabinet, trying to find ways to plug growing holes in the budget deficit and preserve unity in his ruling coalition.

But President Jacques Chirac of France, a nuclear power like China, Russia and the United States, was looking overseas. He was trying to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe in eastern Zaire by proposing a multinational force to ensure the security of refugees there.
He told a news conference at a Franco-Spanish summit in Marseille that a force proposed by Paris and Madrid would need the approval of the U.N. Security Council.

If aliens needed a guiding light, they can rely on Britons sending firework rockets into the night sky every November 5 to celebrate the thwarting of conspirator Guy Fawkes's 17th century Gunpowder Plot to blow up their parliament.
Or there's another science-fiction omen for the scenario.... A giant lake under Europe's largest glacier in Iceland has flooded after a volcanic eruption beneath the ice cap.
A rising torrent threatens to sweep all before it...
